situation:
You are the market planner for BRIGHTSCREEN REPAIR, a shop that fixes phones and laptops from a storefront on the town's main street. The founder (judge) opened the shop nine years ago, has run it profitably every year since, and intends to sell the business and step away within a year. The founder (judge) has asked you to recommend which of two expansion offers the shop should turn down.

A resort hotel group has offered BRIGHTSCREEN REPAIR a service kiosk in three of its properties, serving guests whose phones fail while they are travelling. The offer pays a guaranteed monthly fee, but its contract carries an exclusivity clause covering the whole tourist district, so the shop could serve no other location inside that district for three years.

The founder (judge) has already signed a letter of intent with the developer of a new downtown food hall, which sits inside that same district. A counter there would put the shop in front of everyday local customers while they are choosing where to eat and what to order, and would carry the plain, well-lit look and the neighborhood name the main street storefront is known for.

The two contracts cannot both be honored. Taking the hotel kiosk brings a guaranteed monthly fee that is steady and makes the business easiest to sell to a buyer next year, and it means telling the food hall developer no and giving up the everyday local customers who come in while they are choosing where to eat. Opening the food hall counter keeps those customers and the shop's standing in the neighborhood, and gives up the guaranteed monthly fee.

The founder (judge) wants you to explain how the shop should plan its marketing around whichever market it keeps, to say which offer should be declined, and to say who carries the cost of that choice. The founder (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and after you have presented and answered questions, the founder (judge) will thank you for your time.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the founder (judge) of BRIGHTSCREEN REPAIR, preparing to sell the shop and step away within a year. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have asked your market planner to explain how the shop should plan its marketing around whichever market it keeps, to recommend which of the two offers — the resort hotel group's kiosk or the food hall counter — should be declined, and to say who carries the cost of that choice.

You will greet the participant and ask to hear their ideas. After the participant has presented, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Who ends up paying for this decision?
Can you defend that to them?
